summary: This RFC introduces the Host-Front End Protocol, described in detail in RFC 929. It was designed by a committee of experienced designers for the DoD, with the intent that it be tested through multiple implementations and revised.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 928 introduces the Host-Front End Protocol, a way for a computer to hand its network protocol work to a separate processor. The host then talks to that processor over a simple command interface instead of running TCP, Telnet and the rest itself. The document explains why the idea was proposed, what the protocol looks like, and which questions were still open.

questions: what is the host front end protocol
why move network protocols out of a host
what are the three layers of h-fp
subtitle: The Host-Front End Protocol: moving a machine's network protocol work into a separate processor.

tldr.problem: A host that runs its network protocols itself spends processor time and memory on them, and has to be updated whenever one of those protocols changes. The DoD wanted a standard way to move that work into a separate processor.
tldr.mechanism: The Host-Front End Protocol lets a host talk to an outboard processor that runs the network protocols for it. It has three layers: a Link layer that carries bits, a Channel layer that multiplexes connections and controls flow, and a Command layer whose commands and responses are ASCII strings rather than binary headers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 928 is an introduction, not a specification, and it says so plainly: this is a proposal, not a final standard, and the designers ask for test implementations. The protocol itself is described in RFC 929.

facts.label: Command layer encoding
facts.value: ASCII strings, responses as ASCII-encoded numbers

facts.label: Layers the model offloads
facts.value: ARPANET Reference Model layers II and I, with layer III allowed

today: RFC 928 is an introduction to a proposed protocol rather than a specification, and it says so itself: the document declares that this is a proposal, not a final standard, and asks readers who can write test implementations to do so and coordinate with the author. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category.

sections.title: Why a Front End Protocol
sections.content:
The idea has an origin story the author tells at length. In late May 1971 he was reporting on whether the Multics ARPANET implementation would be ready for a deadline, and a discussion of the Multics NCP, the Network Control Program, which is a blanket term covering the Host-Host and Host-IMP protocol interpreters, led to the question of why the NCP did not queue requests for connections. The answer from the person he was talking to was that he was working on the High-Speed Modular IMP, later the Pluribus IMP. The author's reaction was that, since there was now space to program in the IMP, most of the NCP could be separated out and done outboard, because the only thing that really matters in the host is associating sockets with processes.

Common implementations of the bit-level work in the IMPs would, the author argues, remove disputes over the interpretation of the specification and save host processor cycles. The outboard processing idea has since been called Network Front Ends and, more recently, Outboard Processing Environments, the name change being intended to keep the term distinct from traditional communications front ends, which have nothing to do with protocol interpreters.

The memo does not claim outboard processing is the only way to do intercomputer networking. It argues that attaching a host by emulating a device it already knows, such as a terminal, gets in the way of the process-to-process and procedure-to-procedure communication that makes interesting applications possible, because operating systems make built-in assumptions about known devices. Outboarding also helps where processor cycles or memory are scarce, and even for powerful workstations it avoids having to write a new implementation of an entire protocol suite for every new system, assuming the Host-Front End protocol is noticeably less complex than the protocols it offloads.

Four advantages are listed. Common implementations of a protocol suite are automatically consistent with each other, and in the DoD context it is far easier to procure common implementations of standard protocols than different ones per host type. The resources being shared are the participating hosts' processor cycles and memories, and these are conserved by doing as much of the networking as possible in the front end. Having a front end insulates a host against changes in the offloaded protocols, or even against a change of protocol, so that a host could move from TCP as its Host-Host protocol to, say, ECMA Class 4 as its transport protocol without taking particular cognizance of the change. And for network security architectures that depend on controlling all means of egress from and ingress to the net, uniform use of front ends is clearly desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: Running network protocols inside a big computer uses up that computer's processor time and memory, and means every upgrade of the protocols means upgrading every computer. The proposal is to move the protocol work into a separate small processor and let the computer talk to it over a simple interface. That saves resources, keeps the computer working when the protocols change, and gives one consistent implementation of each protocol across the network.

sections.title: The Three Layers of H-FP
sections.content:
The first point on which the designers reached consensus is that a Host-Front End protocol has three separable layers. At the bottom there must be some physical means for conveying bits from host to front end and back. Because the host's convenience is paramount in outboard processing, what this physical layer is can vary: a bit-serial interface is customary, but parallel or DMA interfaces are fair game if available for the host and usable with a given front end.

In the middle there must be a layer that manages the multiplexing of network connections and the control of flow between host and front end. If the lowest layer is called the Link and the middle layer the Channel, then the Link and Channel layers together are responsible for reliably conveying the bits between host and front end. An outboarded host should not be weaker than one with an inboard implementation of a robust Host-Host protocol such as TCP. A host that comes with a suitable implementation of the X.25 interface protocol could satisfy the requirements of the lower two layers if the front end were conditioned to accept it, though the protocol specification itself details an alternative, less cumbersome channel layer for hosts that do not have or want X.25.

The top layer is the most important and is called the Command layer. This is where the peer Host-Front End modules in the host and the front end communicate with each other, and it is here that the commands and responses are defined. The use of the phrase commands and responses is significant: for the protocol to be proposed for DoD standardisation, unlike all but one of its predecessors, binary encoded headers are not employed. The H-FP commands are ASCII strings, and the responses, following the practice of ARPANET FTP, are ASCII-encoded numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has three parts. The bottom layer moves the bits between the computer and the front end. The middle layer keeps several network connections apart and controls the rate of data flowing between them, so that the two ends agree on how much each can send. The top layer carries the commands that ask the front end to open, use and close those connections, and those commands are written in plain text rather than in binary.

sections.title: The Questions the Proposal Left Open
sections.content:
The memo lists the points that were still open or that needed emphasis. The command approach is the most striking feature to anyone who has seen older front-end protocols: character-oriented commands rather than the more conventional binary-oriented headers at the Command layer. The primary motivation was the report that the approach worked well in an H-FP for the Platform Network called NAP, the Network Access Protocol. Additional rationales came from discussions with the originator of the DCA/DTI H-FP, probably the best known front-end protocol at the time and the one that furnished the default channel layer for the new one: the text approach makes parsing for the ends of variable-length parameters easier, and it allows for the possibility of creating a terminal-supporting front end in a straightforward fashion. The memo also notes that there is nothing sacred about binary headers, and that a reaction of it feels funny is not compelling.

Whether X.25 works is a bigger worry than how the text feels, because many system proprietors would prefer to use off-the-shelf software and hardware. But it is by no means clear that any vendor-supplied X.25 would automatically be usable as a new H-FP channel and link layer, since it all depends on how host programs are able to invoke X.25 on particular systems, and there might be peculiarities in the handling of some constructs. The memo therefore does not claim more than that the new H-FP Command Layer should fit on top of X.25 in a host such that a suitably crafted front end could look like a DCE to low-level host software.

Whether to alter the header structure of the DCA/DTI channel layer is a delicate decision. On the con side, implementations exist and it is well specified. On the pro side, keeping the header as it is is wasteful and the specification will have to be revised anyway to remove what no longer applies. The syntax of the command lines is another point for close scrutiny: the designers took their best shot but make no claim that it is the best possible way to express things, and ask for comments and alternatives.

Offloading of process and application layer protocols is allowed, against the expectations of some. Both Bailey and Grossman had reported favourably on the feasibility, though a given implementation is free not to offload a given layer III protocol, and the designers acknowledge they were feeling their way on the syntax of that part.

On security, the conclusion of a detailed discussion with part of the Blacker design team was that security is to be an aspect of an enhanced H-FP rather than the standard one. Hosts that are not multilevel secure have no legitimate need to tell their front end what their current System High or Dedicated Mode level is; that information should come from a trusted part of a network security architecture. Hosts that are multilevel secure can assert the level of a transmission, and their front ends need a way of learning it, but it is not clear that the host-side protocol interpreter, the channel interpreter and the link interpreter would all be trustworthy, so the labelling is expected to be handled by trusted code in both host and front end, inserted into the normal processing route, that places the label in a known position in the transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The designers list what they were unsure about. Writing the commands as text rather than binary is the biggest change from earlier front ends, and they want reviewers to push back if they have good reasons. They also worry about whether the X.25 standard can be reused for the lower layers, they are not sure the channel layer header should keep its old shape, and they want comments on the command syntax. On security they decide that labelling belongs in a separate enhanced version of the protocol rather than in the standard one.

sections.title: What the Protocol Does Not Decide
sections.content:
The memo also lists what it declares to be non-issues: things people had worried about that the designers consider either outside the protocol or already settled. Who builds front ends is not the protocol's business, except in hoping that a few volunteers will write test implementations of what is at present only a paper protocol. The protocol does not dictate how a vendor must behave beyond what the protocol itself implies: a front end that does not offload SMTP ought to respond with the appropriate Function not implemented code, and disputes over what X.25 is are between the vendor and the customer, not the specification's business. A front end is supposed to offload common protocols in a common fashion, so a given front end should be able to interoperate with another host irrespective of whether that host even has a front end. A protocol specification is not an implementation specification.

Whether only the host can begin a connection, or the front end can also take the initiative, had been disputed for almost as long as front ends had existed. The author resolves it in favour of including the ability for the front end to begin a connection, since there is a compelling reason: a multilevel secure front end that uses a security kernel and a process per level needs to listen for incoming connection requests from the network itself rather than have the host tell it to. Any host that does not need to deal with such begins does not have to, and just has to answer with the correct Function not implemented code.

Routing to one of several front ends when a host has more than one is a non-issue at the protocol level. If the host-side protocol interpreter gets a No resources response to a begin, it can go to another front end if it wants to; the conceptual model is a host and one front end, which ought to be expandable to carry more load at some level. The operator interface to a specific front end is likewise outside the protocol, beyond the provision for Shutdown coming responses as a reflection of an operator action most operator interfaces would provide.
sections.plainLanguage: Some questions that people raise are settled by saying they are not the protocol's business. Who builds the front end, and what its operator interface looks like, are left to vendors. The protocol does allow a front end to open a connection towards the host, because a front end running a security kernel may need to listen for incoming requests itself. And if a host has several front ends, choosing between them is left to the host.

sections.title: Fine Points and Host Integration
sections.content:
Two fine points are called out. The first is the Allocate event in the TCP specification. The author's view is that the specification is wrong in declaring a mandatory interface event whereby the user of a TCP implementation lets it know how much data it can take: in a virtual memory environment with segment sharing, or with a distributed supervisor, all that passed at the interface might be a pointer. One moral is that an interface to an interpreter of a protocol is not the protocol. The other is that the interface to the host-side H-FP protocol interpreter is hard to say much about, but is where the equivalent functionality will be found if TCP has been offloaded: it is reasonable to let the user tell the outboard implementation at begin time whether big or small buffers are expected, but the outboard implementation is expected to deliver bits to the host as they come unless throttled by the channel layer.

The second is precedence. The existence of a notion of precedence in DoD protocols has to be reflected in the outboard implementation, but what role it has in H-FP itself is by no means clear. If the host is full up on the number of server Telnet connections it will handle, what should happen if a high precedence SYN comes in on the Telnet well-known socket? Probably the front end should arbitrarily close a low precedence connection to make room and signal the host. Precedence needs further study, but that should not stop the rest of the protocol from working.

The longest part of the memo is a note on host integration, which the author calls the most important thing about hosts in any intercomputer network, since hosts furnish the resources to be shared. The significant obstacle is that almost invariably they were designed assuming the host was a fully autonomous entity, so few operating systems expect to be members of a heterogeneous community. The sketch given is of the Multics integration of the original ARPANET NCP, which is functionally equivalent to an H-FP protocol interpreter for offloading ARPANET Reference Model layers II and I, together with Telnet.

In Multics each process has a very large segmented virtual memory, where memory references other than to the segment at hand, which can be up to 256K 36-bit words long, indirect through a descriptor segment. Because the code is pure procedure, a distributed supervisor approach is natural: each process appears to have a copy of each procedure segment in its address space. A distinguished process, the Answering Service, fields interrupts from terminals and creates processes after authenticating them, and other shared resources are managed by processes generically known as daemons. Device driver code resides at least in part in the supervisor, and because interrupt time processing can only be performed by supervisor segments, both the IMP-Host protocol interpreter and the multiplexing and demultiplexing aspects of the Host-Host protocol interpreter also live in the supervisor.

For the network daemon, which initially owns all sockets, the control link traffic is relegated to a network daemon process, while normal reads and writes are done by the appropriate user process, so that a supervisor call interface to the NCP is available to procedures within user processes. Reads are inherently asynchronous, and Multics has an event mechanism that lets the calling process decide whether to block when it reads the network. In the version of Unix on which an early front end was based, native I/O was always synchronous, so that system's user Telnet had to consist of two processes. Well-known sockets are handled by having the Answering Service call on the NCP at system initialisation to become the process listening on them. The memo concludes that the key issue in attaching hosts to networks is not what sort of hardware is required, but how the protocol interpreters are made to interrelate with the pre-existing environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo closes with a long worked example: how the original ARPANET network control program was fitted into the Multics operating system, since the two are functionally alike. Multics gave the network code its own protected place in the system and gave each program a way to call it, and it needed a special process to handle the control channel. The lesson is that the hard part of moving networking out of a computer is not the protocol but fitting it into the operating system, and the memo is careful to say that H-FP is not a free lunch.
